headline: Slack Water Lies: Why I Wait Past Midnight for the Inlet to Turn
subhead: The outgoing after 1 a.m. is holding bass in the deep hole, weakfish are stacking under the bridge lights, and the canal locks are still the best-kept secret in the bay.
body_markdown:
I don't leave the dock until the boat traffic dies and the running lights thin out. That's the whole trick to this time of year — the inlet by day is a highway of head boats and jet skis, and the bass that live in that deep hole on the west side just shut down and sulk on the bottom until the noise stops. So I wait. I want the tide to be at least two hours into the outgoing before I drop anchor, and I want it dark enough that the only light on the water is what's bouncing off the Ponquogue Bridge pilings a mile up the bay.

That patience has been paying off. Water's sitting warm — mid-to-upper 70s inshore, and with days like we've had this week, the bass have gone strictly nocturnal. Daytime, they're pinned to structure in the deep water, not interested in much of anything. But once that sun drops and the current starts ripping out through the inlet, they climb up out of that hole and start working the current seams where the bait gets squeezed through the rocks. I've been live-lining bunker on a fish-finder rig, 3 to 4 feet of leader, right along the north jetty where the outgoing current sets up a hard seam against the rock. Eels have worked just as well — snag one on a plain hook, no weight, let it swim naturally in that current, and don't set the hook until you feel the fish load up the rod, not just a tap. Slot fish mostly, a few pushing past 32 inches, nothing enormous yet, but steady enough that two or three rods in the water for two hours after the turn will put fish in the boat most nights this week.

We flagged this pattern last week before it showed up — said that as the tides softened heading into the neap, bass would compress into the strongest current windows and push deeper onto structure, and that's exactly what's happening. The tide range is narrowing hard into the August 5-6 neap, and I've noticed the current at the inlet just isn't ripping the way it was two weeks ago. That means shorter bite windows, but more concentrated ones. If you're fishing the inlet this week, don't spread yourself over four hours of tide — pick the strongest hour of the ebb, usually right around max current about two hours after the turn, and fish it hard. Everything else is filler.

Ponquogue Bridge has been the most reliable thing I've fished all month, honestly. Weakfish are holding tight to the shadow lines under the bridge lights, and they want a slow presentation — half-ounce jig heads with pink or chartreuse Bass Assassins, dropped right into the seam where the light meets the dark water, then just a slow lift-and-drop through the water column. Best window is an hour before the tide turns to outgoing through about an hour into it, when the current is moving enough to hold the bait but not so hard that you're bouncing bottom the whole time. I had four keeper weakfish two nights ago working that exact window, mixed in with a bunch of blues that came through chasing the same bait — small ones mostly, cocktail-size, but they'll hit those same jigs and cut you off if you're not paying attention to your leader.

Daytime, the bay's been about fluke. Nothing spectacular, but honest fishing — drifting the channel edges off Tiana Beach in 12 to 18 feet with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid. The doormat bite everyone's talking about on the ocean side hasn't really translated into the bay yet — what I'm seeing inside is mostly fish in the 16 to 19 inch range, keepers but not the big pool-winning class fish showing up on the open coast. If you want a shot at a real doormat, you need to run out through the inlet on the calmer mornings and work the rips just outside, but with the ocean running a little sloppy this week — three-foot swell out there — that's not a trip for every boat.

The canal's been quiet but not dead. If you time it to the lock openings, that 30 to 45 minute window when the gates start moving water, fluke and the occasional weakfish stack up on the Peconic side waiting for bait to get pushed through. I fished it twice this week and it's the same story both times — dead water, then twenty minutes of real activity right as the current picks up, then it shuts back down. Worth the drive if you're already in Hampton Bays and want a change of scenery, but I wouldn't make a special trip for it right now.

Looking ahead, I'd keep leaning into the dark hours at the inlet through this neap tide — shorter, sharper windows, deep structure, live bait over lures. If the ocean lays down by the weekend I'd take a run out to the rips for fluke before the crowds get out there. And keep an eye on the bunker schools working the beach — if they push into the inlet mouth, the bluefish will find them fast, and that's a daytime show worth chasing with a bucktail or a diamond jig when it happens. Nothing's blitzing yet, but the bait's around, and that's usually all it takes.
